name: Neck training (flexion/extension)

image.caption: US Navy Atlantic Fleet DASH training unit Dam Neck insignia 1965

lead: Neck training means working the neck forward and backward against resistance. Users do it for a thicker, stronger neck that they say complements the jaw, improves posture and gives a more masculine frame.

Resistance exercise loads the neck flexor and extensor muscles. Trials have studied it in other settings: randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared strength and endurance training, a pilot trial tested a six-week program in under-19 rugby players, and a systematic review addressed neck training to reduce head acceleration events in sport. No study has examined it for appearance.

paras: People use towels, hands, plates or machines for forward and backward neck work, usually as a regular part of a lifting routine with gradual progression, and results in size build over months like other muscle training.
No harms were documented in the sources used; forum members raise questions about soreness, asymmetry and sleep apnea without published backing.

chain: More masculine neck, jaw and frame
angle.text: Training the neck forward and back with towels, hands, plates or machines loads the neck muscles, building a thicker, stronger neck that users say complements the jaw, posture and physique. Neck training is studied for pain and sport performance.

lead: Neck training in the flexion and extension sense means exercising the neck forward and backward against resistance, often with a towel, hands, plate or machine. In looksmaxxing forums it is promoted as a way to build a thicker, stronger neck that proponents say complements the jaw, physique and posture.

Published research on neck training mostly addresses chronic neck pain and injury-reduction in sport, not appearance. Randomized trials in women with chronic neck pain compared high-intensity strength and endurance training [1], a pilot trial tested a tailored six-week program in under-19 rugby players [2], and a systematic review and Delphi study addressed neck training aimed at reducing head acceleration events in sport [3]. No study found examined neck training for cosmetic purposes.
infobox: Pain and sport-injury research; none for appearance

paras: A randomized study of 180 women with chronic neck pain assigned participants to high-intensity strength training, local muscle endurance training or a control group, and evaluated changes in neck strength, pain and disability, with a one-year follow-up [1]. Other work has explored how experimental neck pain and training affect motor cortex excitability [4][5][6].

A randomized pilot study in 34 male rugby players aged 16 to 18 assessed a tailored six-week neck conditioning program for strength, fatigue and range of motion [2]. A 2023 analysis examined injury-reduction programs containing neuromuscular neck exercises and soccer head and neck injuries [7], and a 2025 systematic review and Delphi consensus study addressed neck training to reduce head acceleration events [3].

A forum guide presents neck exercises as giving a thicker, stronger neck that goes with the physique and could improve posture and a 'high T' look, and describes forward and backward movements performed with a towel over the head [8]. Replies in that thread say that slow, stretch-focused repetitions can work without added weight [8].

Other members ask about frequency and repetitions, whether training one side more would cause asymmetry, and why months of training showed no visible change [9][10]. A thread titled around sleep apnea indicates that members also discuss possible airway concerns [11].
No studies found on neck flexion and extension training for cosmetic appearance. Trials exist for chronic neck pain [1] and for sport populations [2][3][7], but they do not measure looks.

lore.intro: Neck training is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, discussed as a way to improve overall look and sometimes as a complement to jaw work [8][12].
